newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Moody's sees strong chance of EMU on time.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Moody's sees strong chance of EMU on time.

text.p: Credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service said on Thursday it was highly probable European economic and monetary union will start on time in 1999.
"We try to factor in a variety of scenarios, but the highest probability (is) that EMU will go ahead on time," David Levey, co-head of Moody's sovereign risk unit, told Reuters.
Levey's comments followed a detailed study by Moody's on the implications of monetary union for the credit ratings of participating countries.
The agency concluded that the foreign currency debt ceilings for countries joining EMU would be Aaa, the highest rating possible, signalling the lowest investment risk.
Moody's said that "together, the potential first-round entrants comprise a net creditor bloc".
That would mean that should countries such as Finland and Belgium enter EMU in the first wave, their foreign currency debt rating ceilings would rise from to Aaa from their present Aa1.

Levey said Moody's was currently "pretty certain" that Finland and Belgium would be two of eight countries in the first wave of EMU. The others would likely be Austria, France, Germany, Netherlands, Ireland and Luxembourg.
The start of EMU, scheduled for January 1, 1999, has sparked widespread research on the implications for credit risk in European countries.
The Moody's report follows similar surveys on EMU from rival rating agencies Standard & Poor's and IBCA last year.
Levey said the momentum behind the move to a single European currency ensured there was only the smallest probablility that the process would collapse altogether.
"There's a strong dynamic pushing the process forward...but we're not basing our ratings on absolute certainty -- we're hedging our bets," he said.
Moody's said that while foreign currency debt ceilings would be the top Aaa investment grade, that was not necessarily the case for each member's domestic currency debt.

"On the EMU start date, Moody's rating on each member's domestic currency debt will become that government's rating for debt denominated in euros," Moody's said in its report, adding that euros effectively become the local curency.

Explaining the rationale for the government bond ratings, Levey said EMU-bloc governments would likely benefit from the broadening of the European capital market since investors will no longer worry about foreign exchange risk within the bloc.
But he added that for some governments joining EMU, the benefits associated with the loss of foreign exchange risk may be outweighed by the loss of prime creditor status within their own countries.
When a government is the prime creditor in its own currency, banks, institutional investors and other capital suppliers tend to support their own government in times of financial stress.

"But when foreign exchange risk disappears, lenders (investors) will no longer have a clear preference for bonds of their own governments and an important financial safety net will be weakened," Levey said.
He said differing yields between participating countries' government bonds would primarily be determined by credit risk.
"The credibility of government policy will be extremely important," he said.
Levey said British sovereign ratings were unlikely to be affected if the UK stayed out of EMU.
"I don't think there's any chance that the UK...will be affected even if it stays outside of EMU," Levey said.
Britain, which remains indecisive about whether to commit itself to EMU, currently has Aaa sovereign ratings from Moody's for both its foreign currency and local currency debt.
